speaker: N
text: In 1945, a man invented a new way to cook because a chocolate bar melted in his pocket.

speaker: N
text: His name was Percy Spencer, and he had never even finished school.

speaker: N
text: But he built radar parts for the war, and he was brilliant at it.

speaker: N
text: One day, standing next to a humming radar tube, he felt something sticky.

speaker: N
text: His chocolate bar had turned to goo.

speaker: N
text: The room wasn't hot.

speaker: N
text: He wasn't hot.

speaker: N
text: So he sent someone out for a bag of popcorn kernels.

speaker: N
text: He held them near the tube, and they burst all over the lab.

speaker: N
text: Next, he tried an egg.

speaker: N
text: It wobbled, shook, and exploded right in a coworker's face.

speaker: N
text: Meanwhile, the war was ending, and his factory's thousands of radar tubes were about to become useless.

speaker: N
text: You see, that radar tube was firing out invisible microwaves.

speaker: N
text: And microwaves make the tiny water molecules inside food spin back and forth, billions of times a second.

speaker: N
text: All that jiggling turns into heat, right inside the food.

speaker: N
text: That's why the snack got hot, but the room didn't.

speaker: N
text: So his company turned a war machine into a kitchen machine.

speaker: N
text: The first one was taller than a man and weighed as much as a piano.

speaker: N
text: It cost about five thousand dollars.

speaker: N
text: Today, almost every kitchen has one.

speaker: N
text: Not bad for a guy with no diploma and a ruined snack.

speaker: N
text: And it all started when...
